title: The man they called trustworthy
told: from the early biographies and the hadith

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? who holds the spare key to your home?
options: of course. the one you’re surest of. listen.
then you know what trust feels like. listen.
that’s okay. today is about the kind of person you’d give it to.

steps.line: Long ago in Mecca, the clans rebuilt the Ka‘ba, the old house of worship. When it came to setting the sacred Black Stone back, they nearly came to blows.
Every clan wanted the honor. So, the early biographies say, they agreed: the next man through the gate would decide.

steps.q: The next man through was Muhammad ﷺ, years before his calling. What do you think he did?
o: Gave the honor to the oldest clan
Had every clan lift it together
steps.why: He spread a cloak, and every clan held a corner. No one won, so no one lost face.

steps.line: He spread out a cloak, set the stone in the middle, and asked a man from each clan to take a corner. Together they lifted it.

steps.q: He was about thirty-five then, already known for honest dealing. What was his trade?
steps.why: He led trading caravans, among them Khadija’s. The early biographies say her trust in his honesty is part of why she proposed marriage.

steps.line: Years later, he climbed the hill of Safa and called the clans together. “If I told you riders in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me?”
“Yes,” they said. “We have never known you to lie.” Then he gave them his message, and many turned away.

steps.q: Why did he start with a question about riders in the valley, before giving his message?
o: To test whether they were listening
To have them say his record out loud
To warn them of a real attack coming
steps.why: Their own answer, “we’ve never known you to lie,” came before his message. He let his life speak first.

steps.line: Even so, the early biographies say, many who refused his message still left their valuables in his care. Trusted first. Believed, by many, only later.

steps.q: Years later he had to leave Mecca in secret. What did he do about the valuables people had left with him?
o: Left ‘Ali behind to return each one
Took them along to keep them safe
Gave them to the poor of Mecca
steps.why: The early biographies say ‘Ali stayed behind to hand every item back, even to people plotting against the Prophet ﷺ.

steps.line: Today, someone hands a neighbor the spare key. Not to the most impressive person they know. To the one who has never let them down.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. before most people believed his message, a whole city already trusted him with their things.
in islam, the prophet ﷺ is known through words, never pictures. the qur’an calls his character tremendous, and muslims ask peace on him whenever his name is said.

steps.q: The people on the hill said “we’ve never known you to lie,” then refused his message. What does that tell you about trust and belief?
o: Trust and belief are really the same thing
You can trust someone long before believing them
Once they refused him, the trust was gone
steps.why: They kept leaving their valuables with him. Trust came first. Belief, for many, came later.

today.say: today, keep one small promise you’ve been putting off: the call, the book to return, the message you said you’d send. the qur’an praises those who keep their trusts and their promises, and al-amin was a name built one kept promise at a time.
options: lovely. that’s how trust is built.

Musnad Ahmad 15504 (al-Sa’ib ibn ‘Abd Allah: the Black Stone, the cloak and the clans)

Sahih al-Bukhari 4770; Sahih Muslim 208 (on Mount Safa: “If I told you that cavalry were in the valley about to attack you, would you believe me?” “We have only known you to tell the truth”), after Qur’an 26:214
Ibn Hisham: at the hijra, ‘Ali stayed behind to return the deposits people had left with him
Qur’an 68:4 (“And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature,” Pickthall)
Qur’an 33:56 (asking blessings and peace on the Prophet)
Qur’an 23:8 (“And who are shepherds of their pledge and their covenant,” Pickthall)
